subject: english-literature
title: Spivak and the Subaltern
welcome_lead: Whose voice survives the archive? Spivak's question still echoes — can the subaltern speak?
meta_desc: Spivak's subaltern, strategic essentialism and post-colonial theory at A-Level.
final_note: You have read with Spivak — and seen how representation can silence even when it intends to amplify.

concepts.def: Gayatri Spivak — those outside hegemonic discourse, whose speech is mediated, translated and often distorted.
Spivak's foundational essay examining the impossibility of hearing the subaltern within colonial archives.
Spivak's term for the political use of essentialist categories despite their theoretical problems.
Heidegger via Spivak — how a Western text imaginatively constitutes the colonised world.
The violence of imposing Western categories on non-Western knowledges, erasing local frameworks.
Spivak argues every translation across cultural boundaries risks losing voice.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Spivak's essay (1988) examines the case of Bhubaneswari Bhaduri, whose suicide tried to leave a feminist anti-colonial message that her family could not read.

Even the most sympathetic Western intellectual risks speaking for rather than letting subaltern voices speak.
Spivak coined strategic essentialism for the political need to deploy categories like 'women' or 'colonised peoples' even while critiquing them theoretically.
In a separate essay Spivak reads Brontë, Rhys and Mary Shelley alongside imperialism — Bertha Mason in Jane Eyre as the colonial subaltern.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator's views are always the author's views.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Postmodernism means writing about the future.

mcqs.q: Why are genre conventions important when interpreting a text?
options: The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Genre means whether a book is fiction or non-fiction.
They set reader expectations the text can fulfil or subvert; analysing how a text uses or breaks conventions reveals its meaning and significance.
Genre is just a label to help bookshops categorise novels.
Self-aware metafiction, intertextuality, scepticism toward grand narratives, playfulness with form, and blurring of high/low culture.
Postmodernism means writing about the future.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Postmodernism just means literature written after modernism.
